directAnswer: Liberius was pope from 352 to 366, during the struggle between the Nicene faith and the Arian-leaning policies of Emperor Constantius II. He refused at first to condemn St. Athanasius and was exiled to Thrace, but ancient writers report that he later made concessions that allowed him to return to Rome. He is the earliest pope not listed as a saint in the Latin Church, though Eastern Christians honor him on August 27.

paras: When Liberius became pope in 352, Constantius II ruled the whole empire and was determined to secure the condemnation of Athanasius of Alexandria. Councils at Arles in 353 and Milan in 355 bowed to imperial pressure, and even the papal legates at Arles gave way.

Liberius refused to add his name. He insisted that Athanasius could not be condemned without a fair hearing and that the faith of Nicaea must be upheld. In 355 he was seized, brought before the emperor, and sent into exile at Beroea in Thrace. In his absence, the archdeacon Felix was installed in Rome, a figure the Church later counted as an antipope.

Liberius returned to Rome in 358. Writers such as Athanasius, Hilary of Poitiers, and Jerome report that the hardships of exile wore him down and that he accepted the condemnation of Athanasius and signed a creed drafted at Sirmium that avoided the Nicene language. Which formula he signed, and whether letters attributed to him from this period are authentic, remain debated by historians.

The Catholic tradition has noted that whatever Liberius signed under duress was not a free act of teaching addressed to the whole Church. The episode was nonetheless remembered as a painful moment, and it is one reason he was never added to the Roman calendar of saints.

sections.h2: Return to Rome and Reconciliation with Nicaea
paras: Romans welcomed Liberius back enthusiastically, and Felix was soon forced out. After Constantius died in 361, Liberius openly supported the Nicene faith once more. He worked to reconcile bishops who had compromised at the Council of Rimini in 359, provided they now professed the creed of Nicaea.
Near the end of his life, he received a delegation of Eastern bishops who accepted the Nicene Creed and restored them to communion, a sign of how far the tide had turned.

sections.h2: The Liberian Basilica and the Liberian Catalogue
paras: Liberius is credited with a basilica on the Esquiline Hill, known as the Basilica Liberiana. The present Santa Maria Maggiore was built in the following century under Sixtus III, and the story of a miraculous August snowfall marking its site is a medieval legend.

His name also survives in the Liberian Catalogue, a list of popes ending with him that was included in a Roman calendar compiled in 354. It is one of the most valuable early sources for papal chronology. Liberius died on September 24, 366, and the disputed election that followed led to violent conflict between the supporters of Damasus and Ursinus.

keyFacts: Exiled to Beroea in Thrace in 355 for refusing to condemn St. Athanasius
Ancient writers report he yielded to imperial pressure before returning in 358
Gave his name to the Liberian Catalogue, an early list of popes
Not on the Latin calendar of saints; honored in the East on August 27

faqs.question: Why is Pope Liberius not a saint in the Catholic Church?
faqs.answer: He is not listed in the Roman Martyrology, largely because of reports that he gave in to Emperor Constantius II during his exile. Eastern Christian churches, however, venerate him as a saint.

faqs.question: Did Pope Liberius teach heresy?
faqs.answer: Ancient sources say he signed an ambiguous creed and condemned Athanasius under duress, but the details are disputed. It was not a free, formal teaching to the Church, and after his return he again supported the Nicene faith.

faqs.question: Is Santa Maria Maggiore the Liberian Basilica?
faqs.answer: Santa Maria Maggiore is often linked to the Basilica Liberiana, but the present church was built under Pope Sixtus III in the fifth century. The snow legend about its founding is a later tradition.
